query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles, thermally induced local chemical heterogeneity—manifested as both variations in atomic ordering in the core and modest segregation (especially at surfaces) of lower‐melting constituents—governs the premelting and melting behavior by creating spatial differences in local bonding strength and energy barriers.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid-solution nanoparticles of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu synthesized under conditions (e.g., rapid cooling) that yield a nominally homogeneous elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Controlled, incremental heating of the nanoparticles in an inert atmosphere across the temperature window from the onset of premelting to full melting.
generation.conditions: In situ thermal analysis (using techniques such as TEM or DSC) on particles of uniform size and under identical inert environmental conditions to isolate the thermal effects on local chemical configuration.
generation.structural_mediator: Local variations in chemical ordering and subtle elemental segregation (with lower-melting species tending to accumulate at surfaces).
generation.mechanism: As the nanoparticles are heated, limited atomic mobility promotes enhanced local ordering in some regions while allowing slight segregation of lower-melting-point elements at the surface. Regions with stronger local ordering maintain higher cohesive energy and melt more abruptly at higher temperatures, whereas areas with segregation lower the local energy barrier for phase transition, initiating premelting over an extended temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles that experience conditions favoring enhanced atomic ordering (e.g., via slower or controlled heating) will exhibit a sharper melting transition at a relatively higher temperature compared to nanoparticles that maintain or develop more pronounced local segregation, which will display an earlier onset of premelting and a broader melting interval.
generation.baseline: HEA nanoparticles produced under standard rapid cooling conditions that yield a uniform, homogeneous elemental distribution.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoscale Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu particles under inert thermal conditions over the temperature regime spanning from initial surface softening (premelting) to complete liquefaction; effects may differ for bulk materials or systems where size and external pressures dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While it is clear that local chemical heterogeneity impacts melting behavior, the relative contributions of internal ordering versus surface segregation—and how these effects scale with particle size and precise heating rates—remain to be quantitatively determined.

This behavior contrasts with the bimetallic case, suggesting that the rules governing phase formation differ for the systems containing two or five elements: Single-phase alloy formation occurs more readily if more elements are present, as systems that are immiscible on the bimetallic level can be driven to mix by introducing more elements. As the resulting phases of the binary particles cannot readily be explained by their thermodynamic stability, we devised a kinetic model to rationalize the experimental results based on the restrictions imposed by the synthesis. This will make it increasingly difficult for elements with strong preferences of ordering to form an intermetallic structure or for elements that repulse each other to segregate, simply because they are more dilute. Our work provides direct visualization of nanoparticles on amorphous carbon supports and elucidate the details of amorphous carbon graphitization during ultrafast exposure to extremely high temperatures under electrical Joule heating process. The in situ TEM studies of Joule heating on amorphous carbon fibers loaded with metal precursors show that during the Joule heating process, the CNFs undergo volumetric expansion due to amorphous to crystalline phase transition, which is also associated with formation and stabilization of metallic nanoparticles on the carbon supports. The crystallized CNFs are made of T-graphite with a high density of randomly dispersed edge planes. These edge planes are highly defective and act as preferred sites for the nucleation of metallic nanoparticles. In addition, metal atoms diffuse into layered structure strengthening the anchoring of the nanoparticles on the edge planes. This prevents the nanoparticles from further aggregation at extremely high temperatures as confirmed by MD simulation and in situ heating in TEM. drafts.hypothesis: In high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles, premature surface melting is triggered by nanoscale chemical segregation where certain regions become enriched in lower-melting-point elements, leading to a locally reduced energy barrier for the phase transition.
drafts.material_initial_state: Initially, the nanoparticles are a chemically homogeneous, solid-solution high-entropy alloy of iron, nickel, chromium, cobalt, and copper.
drafts.intervention: Expose the nanoparticles to a controlled ramped heating protocol across the premelting and melting regime.
drafts.conditions: The experiment should be carried out under an inert atmosphere with identical heat-treatment rates, using nanoparticles of similar size to minimize geometrical/surface effects.
drafts.structural_mediator: Local chemical segregation and clustering that create micro-domains with varying elemental compositions.
drafts.mechanism: Due to the inherent chemical complexity, small fluctuations during synthesis or early heating may lead to local enrichment of lower-melting-point elements (e.g., copper). These regions serve as nucleation sites for premelting because their local bonding environments have lower energy barriers for phase change compared to more homogeneously mixed regions.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles exhibiting even subtle chemical segregation will show an earlier onset of premelting and a broader melting regime (i.e., melting over a wider temperature range) compared to a baseline homogeneous nanoparticle (or an ideal computational model with uniform elemental distribution).
drafts.baseline: A nanoparticle system with a perfectly homogeneous distribution of Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu (as can be approximated either by ideal synthesis or computational stabilization) which would display a sharper melting transition commencing at a higher temperature.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies within the nanoscale regime (where surface-to-volume effects are significant) and primarily within the temperature window from the first detectable signs of surface disorder (premelting) to complete nanoparticle liquefaction. It may not hold for bulk materials or systems where size or external pressure effects dominate.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles: one set processed to enhance chemical homogeneity (e.g., via slow annealing) and one set processed under conditions known to favor local segregation (e.g., rapid cooling). Heat both sets in situ (using transmission electron microscopy heating or differential scanning calorimetry) while measuring the onset and progression of premelting and melting. Use high-resolution elemental mapping (e.g., EDS) to correlate local composition with melting behavior.
measurements: Onset temperature of premelting (detected by surface disorder or partial liquefaction)
Spatial elemental distribution maps via EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles produced under conditions favoring chemical segregation do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in the premelting onset temperature or broader melting interval than the homogeneous ones, or if no correlation is found between local chemical segregation and altered phase transition behavior, then the hypothesis would be refuted.

drafts.hypothesis: Local variations in chemical ordering—specifically, the degree of homogeneous elemental mixing versus local segregation—govern the premelting and melting behavior of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
drafts.material_initial_state: Solid-solution nanoparticles of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu produced under standard synthesis conditions with a nominally random distribution of elements.
drafts.intervention: Application of controlled thermal treatments (altering cooling rates) post-synthesis to induce differences in local chemical ordering.
drafts.conditions: Experiments conducted in situ across the temperature region spanning the onset of premelting to complete melting, ensuring particle size and environmental pressure remain constant.
drafts.structural_mediator: The extent of local chemical ordering and any incipient elemental segregation.
drafts.mechanism: Local chemical ordering alters the atomic bonding environment and energy barriers for atomic rearrangement. Nanoparticles with a higher degree of ordering (obtained by slower cooling rates) have increased cohesive energy locally, leading to a sharper, higher-temperature melting transition and a narrower premelting regime. In contrast, particles with more random mixing (obtained by rapid cooling) display a broader range of premelting behavior due to heterogeneous bond strengths.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (rapidly cooled, more disordered nanoparticles), slowly cooled nanoparticles with enhanced local chemical ordering will exhibit an increased melting temperature and a more abrupt transition from premelting to melting, while the rapidly cooled nanoparticles will show an extended premelting regime with a broader melting profile.
drafts.baseline: HEA nanoparticles synthesized and cooled under standard (rapid cooling) conditions leading to a random, homogeneous elemental distribution.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies to Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles in the nanoscale regime where surface effects are significant but do not overwhelm chemical ordering influences, and within the thermal regime encompassing initial premelting through complete melting.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles from the same synthesis batch. Subject one set to rapid cooling (to maintain random chemical distribution) and the other set to slow cooling (to promote local chemical ordering). Perform in-situ heating experiments (using TEM or differential scanning calorimetry) to record the onset of premelting and the melting profiles. Concurrently, assess the degree of local chemical ordering using atom probe tomography or high-resolution microscopy.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of local chemical ordering (via atom probe or high-res TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slowly cooled nanoparticles do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in melting temperature and a sharper melting profile compared with the rapidly cooled baseline, or if no measurable differences in local chemical ordering are detected despite different cooling protocols, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The premature melting behavior of solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper HEA nanoparticles is governed by the kinetic restrictions on atomic mobility imposed by their multi‐element (high-entropy) composition, which forces a stochastic, highly distorted atomic arrangement that raises the local melting threshold and produces a broadened premelting regime compared to simpler (e.g., bimetallic) systems.
drafts.material_initial_state: Solid, single-phase HEA nanoparticles made from equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios of Fe, Ni, Cr, Co and Cu with significant lattice distortion.
drafts.intervention: Controlled heating through the premelting/melting range using in situ thermal analysis (e.g., TEM or DSC) at carefully tuned heating rates.
drafts.conditions: The nanoparticles should be synthesized under conditions that limit atomic mobility (e.g., low precursor reduction temperatures or rapid quenching) and compared to similarly sized bimetallic or simpler alloy nanoparticles under identical thermal ramps.
drafts.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortion and heterogeneity in bond strengths arising from the random distribution of different atomic radii and bonding characteristics.
drafts.mechanism: Limited atomic mobility due to the multi-element, high-entropy composition forces the atoms to remain in a stochastic, strained arrangement during heating. This kinetic hindrance delays the formation of a uniformly molten phase and produces a broadened, gradual premelting behavior as local melting events occur over a range of temperatures rather than a sharp transition.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to bimetallic nanoparticles of similar size, the HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a broader premelting temperature range, with a delayed onset of full melting observable as a more gradual increase in liquid fraction and associated calorimetric signals.
drafts.baseline: Bimetallic nanoparticles with similar dimensions and comparable synthesis conditions, which are known to exhibit sharper melting transitions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloy nanoparticle systems synthesized under kinetic conditions that severely restrict free atomic diffusion (e.g., solid-state reduction or similar low-mobility precursors) and in which the high configurational entropy is the dominant factor influencing phase evolution.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: one high-entropy alloy (FeNiCrCoCu) and one bimetallic alloy (e.g., FeNi) of comparable sizes and microstructures. Using in situ techniques (such as TEM heating or differential scanning calorimetry), measure the onset and width of the melting transition under identical controlled heating rates.
measurements: Temperature-dependent phase identification (e.g., by XRD or electron diffraction during heating)
Calorimetric heat flow measurements to determine melting onset and peak temperatures
Direct TEM observation of structural changes (e.g., onset of liquid region) in individual nanoparticles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy nanoparticles do not show a significantly broader or delayed premelting/melting transition compared to the bimetallic nanoparticles, or if the melting behavior is identical (after controlling for size and morphology), then the hypothesis that kinetic limitations due to multi-element stochastic mixing govern the premelting behavior would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles, premelting initiates at the surface because the lower–melting–point element (copper) segregates there, forming a liquid‐like layer that catalyzes the nanoparticle’s overall melting.
drafts.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles fabricated as single-phase, solid high-entropy alloys with an initially uniform distribution of Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu.
drafts.intervention: Controlled, incremental heating of the nanoparticles in an inert atmosphere while monitoring structure and composition (e.g., via in situ TEM, DSC, or surface-sensitive spectroscopy).
drafts.conditions: Heating across a temperature range that spans from below the premelting onset to above complete melting, with heating rates slow enough to allow atomic diffusion but avoiding oxidation.
drafts.structural_mediator: A thin, copper-enriched surface layer that forms via thermally activated, preferential segregation.
drafts.mechanism: Due to disparities in elemental melting temperatures and limited atomic mobility in a high-entropy matrix, copper (the lowest-melting component) diffuses toward the surface on heating. This creates local regions with reduced cohesive energy and a lower effective melting point. Once a liquid-like copper-rich layer forms at the surface, it weakens the lattice cohesion locally, thereby promoting progressive melting into the nanoparticle core.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Spectroscopic and microscopy measurements will reveal an early onset of surface softening and liquid-like behavior along with detectable copper enrichment at the surface. Compared to a baseline nanoparticle showing homogeneous melting at a higher, sharper transition temperature, these particles will exhibit a broadened melting interval initiated at the surface.
drafts.baseline: Nanoparticles with a homogeneous elemental distribution that, in the absence of significant segregation, would exhibit a relatively sharp melting point without pronounced premelting behavior.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoparticles in the studied size range (e.g., <50 nm) where surface-to-volume ratios amplify segregation effects and under heating conditions that permit limited atomic mobility without causing oxidation or rapid coalescence.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles and subject them to stepwise heating under identical inert conditions. Employ in situ high-resolution TEM combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping to monitor both morphological changes and surface composition versus temperature. In parallel, record differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) for thermal signatures of phase transitions.
measurements: Surface composition profiles (EDS) as a function of temperature
Onset temperature of premelting as indicated by TEM observations
DSC heat flow curves to determine the breadth and onset of melting
Comparative analysis against nanoparticles synthesized with suppressed copper mobility (e.g., by pre-alloying or surface treatments)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant copper enrichment is detected at the nanoparticle surfaces during the premelting regime, or if the melting transition is sharp and uniform (without evidence of a surface layer initiating melting), then the hypothesis that copper segregation governs premelting is falsified.
